summary:
EARTH TO SPACE: NEW HORIZONS is an open-data interactive platform built by Team QUEBRACHO COSMOS (Santiago del Estero, Argentina) to identify, evaluate, and simulate terrestrial analog sites for Lunar and Martian exploration—specifically the Lunar South Pole (Artemis / Shackleton Crater), Mars Arcadia Planitia, and Mars Jezero Crater.

Going beyond visual similarity or well-known benchmarks like Atacama or McMurdo, our tool combines real NASA POWER satellite climatology, surface soil wetness (GWETTOP), surface albedo, and Copernicus DEM topography (Horn slope and terrain roughness) to score 50 global sites—highlighting 42 under-studied candidates—plus any live coordinate or place name worldwide.

To ensure scientific rigor, our 6-dimensional similarity engine applies physical coherence penalties (zero wind weighting for the lunar vacuum and climate penalties against humid craters) and transparently reports where each analogy breaks down (1.0 G gravity, atmosphere, and magnetospheric shielding). Integrated Engineering Experiment and Environmental Analysis modules let mission teams model rover mobility under 0.165 G / 0.38 G, annual solar-dust budgets, seasonal windows, and COSPAR field protection protocols.
details:
Overview & How It Works

EARTH TO SPACE: NEW HORIZONS is an interactive web platform built in Python and Streamlit that bridges open NASA Earth observations with planetary exploration targets on the Moon and Mars. Rather than treating analog selection as a static visual comparison, the platform operates across six integrated bilingual (English/Spanish) modules:

1. Global Explorer (Live Discovery): Combines NASA GIBS Blue Marble imagery (with Esri World Imagery and OpenStreetMap layers) and OpenStreetMap Nominatim geocoding. Users can search any location worldwide by name, enter custom coordinates, or click directly on the global map to fetch real-time NASA POWER climatology and a 3x3 Copernicus DEM elevation grid (computing Horn slope and terrain roughness) on the fly. A toggle prioritizes 42 under-studied candidates over 8 historical benchmarks.

2. Detailed Site Analysis (Earth vs. Space): Breaks down each site's score transparently across six quantitative dimensions—Cold Extremes, Thermal Amplitude, Aridity & Soil/Albedo, Terrain Topography, Aeolian Dynamics, and Altitude/Pressure/Solar Irradiance—alongside an Astrobiology Stress Index, a 12-month seasonality curve, a real 7x7 3D DEM topographic surface reconstruction, a side-by-side orbital view via NASA Moon/Mars Trek WMTS layers, and a "Scientific Validity & Limitations" diagnostic explaining where the analogy holds, where it fails, and what engineering tests fit the site. Users can export technical reports (.md) and metrics (.csv).

3. Direct Comparison: Compares under-studied analog candidates (e.g., Harrat Khaybar, Salar de Arizaro, Pastos Grandes, Qaidam Basin, Ngari Tibetan Plateau) head-to-head against historical NASA benchmarks (Atacama, Haughton Crater, McMurdo, Askja) using overlaid 6D radar charts and monthly soil-skin temperature curves.

4. Data Laboratory: Enables multivariate filtering by elevation, aridity, slope, and lithology (volcanic basalt, evaporite salar, impact crater, permafrost, hyper-arid regolith) with configurable scatter plots and CSV export.

5. Engineering Experiment Simulator: Translates analog telemetry into actionable hardware testing. Engineers can simulate rover mobility (comparing 1.0 G Earth power and traction forces against 0.165 G on the Moon and 0.38 G on Mars, calculating exact gravity-offload harness mass), run 12-month solar power and aeolian dust-loss budgets, identify optimal seasonal campaign windows, and save/export an Experiment Research Log (.csv).

6. Environmental Analysis & Planetary Protection: Evaluates annual precipitation, topsoil moisture (0–5 cm), aeolian dust-erosion risk, net absorbed solar flux (via surface albedo), and COSPAR-inspired field environmental sensitivity for fragile permafrost, salt-flat extremophile crusts, and hyper-arid terrains.

Scientific Rigor & Factors Considered

We explicitly prevent misleading matches through physical coherence rules:

- Lunar South Pole assigns 0.0 weight to aeolian wind (vacuum environment) and penalizes sites with minimum annual temperatures above 0°C or high rainfall.

- Mars Arcadia Planitia penalizes steep slopes (>10°) and high roughness (>25 m) to preserve flat, ice-bearing plain analogs.

- Mars Jezero Crater enforces hyper-aridity and penalizes humid/rainy craters (>300–350 mm/year), separating purely morphological impact craters from full environmental analogs.

- Every analysis explicitly states universal terrestrial limits: Earth cannot remove 1.0 G gravity, convective atmospheric pressure, or magnetospheric radiation shielding.

Tools, Software & Transparency

- Tech Stack: Python 3.13, Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, Plotly, Folium, streamlit-folium, and Requests (hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud; source code at https://github.com/NicolasGomezPaz/earth-to-space-new-horizons).

- Open Data Integrity: All 50 catalog sites and live coordinate queries fetch real telemetry from public NASA POWER and Open-Meteo Elevation APIs without hardcoded fake climate datasets (for live custom coordinates without monthly catalog records, the simulator transparently flags a sinusoidal seasonal approximation derived from real NASA annual parameters).

- Super Intelligence (SI) Disclosure: AI/LLM coding assistants (Gemini, Antigravity IDE) were used to accelerate Python scaffolding, UI styling, and documentation drafting, and SI-generated visual assets in the slide presentation are labeled accordingly. All planetary constants were cross-checked against NASA mission fact sheets, and all terrestrial telemetry was verified directly against live NASA POWER and Open-Meteo API responses.
